evidence: Plaut. Aul. 184: ubi dīves blandē appellat pauperem
Hor. AP 421: dīves agrīs, dīves positīs in fēnore nummīs, rich in land, rich in money lent at interest
terms.comment: Comparative dītior, superlative dītissimus. As a noun, a rich man; dīvitēs, the rich.

terms.gloss: well-to-do, wealthy; properly, rich in land
evidence: Plaut. Trin. 565: Et ego esse locuplēs, vērum nēquīquam volō
terms.comment: Cicero explains it from land, locus: when wealth lay in cattle and land, men were called pecūniōsī et locuplētēs (Rep. 2.16, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Trin. 493: aequō mendīcus atque ille opulentissimus

phrases.latin: nēmō nāscitur dīves; quisquis exit in lūcem jussus est lacte et pannō esse contentus
phrases.english: No one is born rich: whoever comes out into the light is told to be content with milk and a rag

phrases.latin: Nōn temerārium est, ubi dīves blandē appellat pauperem. jam illic homō aurum scit mē habēre, eō mē salūtat blandius.
phrases.english: It’s no accident when a rich man speaks sweetly to a poor one: he must know I have gold, that’s why he greets me so sweetly.
